passage: When Pooja got off the tempo at the village school gate, two girls near the well looked at her and giggled. In class, someone passed a note behind her. At recess, Irfan, the boy who sat next to her, finally said quietly, "They're saying your father ran off with the money from the dairy." Pooja's face burned. Her father had gone to the city to work, that was all; he called every night. She wanted to crawl under the desk. Then she wanted to grab the note and tear it up in front of everyone. "Who said it?" she asked, her voice shaking. Irfan shrugged. Pooja sat very still, her fists tight in her lap, not knowing which part of the story to fight first.

qa.q: Where had Pooja's father really gone?
qa.a: Her father had gone to the city to work, and he called every night.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling after Irfan told her the rumour?
qa.a: She felt shame and anger at once, wanting to crawl under the desk and also to tear up the note, and confused because part of the story was false. 😠

qa.q: What turning point could help Pooja now?
qa.a: She could tell her teacher or her mother what is being said, so an adult can help stop the story instead of her facing it alone.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel after telling Pooja?
qa.a: He may feel awkward and unsure whether he did right, but perhaps also that she deserved to know.

grounding: It shows a girl noticing stares and giggles, learning a partly false story about her family, and feeling shame, anger and confusion.

passage: The bell rang at Dalia's school in Accra, and as she walked to her locker, two boys stopped talking and grinned. A girl near the stairs covered her mouth. At lunch Kofi slid onto the bench beside her. "Dalia, people say you were caught stealing from the corner shop." Dalia stared at him. Last Saturday she had gone back to the shop to return extra change the owner gave her by mistake. Someone must have seen her at the counter with the owner and made up the rest. Her ears went hot. She wanted to run to the toilets and hide. She also wanted to shout at the whole canteen. Instead, she sat frozen, her rice going cold.

qa.q: Why had Dalia gone back to the corner shop?
qa.a: She went back to return extra change the owner gave her by mistake.

qa.q: How can you tell Dalia feels torn between hiding and hitting back?
qa.a: She wanted to run and hide in the toilets and also to shout at the whole canteen, but instead she sat frozen.

qa.q: What would you advise Dalia to do next?
qa.a: Tell a trusted teacher and her family what is being said, and let the shop owner confirm what really happened, rather than facing the rumour alone.

qa.q: What might Kofi be thinking as he watches Dalia freeze?
qa.a: He may be unsure whether the story is true, and worried that telling her made things worse.

grounding: It illustrates a girl who notices stares and learns a partly false story about her, feeling shame and anger and wanting to hide or hit back.

passage:
I noticed it on Tuesday. Girls stopped talking when I came into the washroom. Two of them giggled behind their hands at assembly.

At lunch my friend Naveen told me, looking at his shoes. "They're saying your father is in jail."

My face went so hot I thought it would melt. My father isn't in jail. He's working on a ship and he comes back in three months. But he once went to the police station to report our stolen cycle. Someone must have seen.

I wanted to hide in the library forever. Then I wanted to hit someone. I didn't know which.

I went home and told Amma everything, crying. She held me and said, "You haven't done anything wrong." The next morning she came with me to see my class teacher, who spoke to the class that same day.

— Sangeeta

qa.q: Where is Sangeeta's father actually?
qa.a: Working on a ship; he comes back in three months.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when Naveen told her the rumour?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt ashamed and angry, face burning, confused because the story was partly based on something real.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped?
qa.a: She listened, comforted Sangeeta, said it wasn't Sangeeta's fault, and went along to the class teacher, who spoke to the class that day.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt telling Sangeeta?
qa.a: He was probably uncomfortable and sorry, looking at his shoes, but wanted Sangeeta to know.

grounding: Sangeeta notices stares and giggles, learns a partly false rumour about her father, and feels shame and anger before turning to her mother and teacher.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 5B, Thursday

In drawing, several children kept glancing at Pooja and giggling. Pooja kept her head down and pressed so hard with her crayon that it snapped.

At break she stayed at her desk. When I sat beside her, she said, very quietly, "They're saying I wet the bed at the class picnic. I didn't. I spilled my water bottle."

Her face was red, and her fists were tight. "I want to hit Rohini. Or never come back."

I told her it was not her fault and that I was glad she told me. I stayed with her through break. Then I spoke to the class, without naming anyone, about how stories get twisted and how they hurt.

I phoned Pooja's mother after school and will watch Rohini's group tomorrow.

— Joseph Sir

qa.q: What had actually happened at the class picnic?
qa.a: Pooja spilled her water bottle.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when she told Joseph Sir?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and angry, wanting to hit Rohini or never come back, and confused because the story was twisted from something real.

qa.q: What did Joseph Sir do that helped?
qa.a: He stayed with Pooja, said it wasn't her fault, spoke to the class about twisted stories, and phoned her mother the same day.

qa.q: How might Rohini's group feel after the class talk?
qa.a: They may feel a little embarrassed or guilty, realising the story wasn't true and was hurting Pooja.

grounding: A teacher's note shows Pooja noticing giggles, learning a partly false rumour and feeling shame and anger, and the teacher's same-day response.

passage:
Friday

Worst day ever.

Everyone was looking at me and giggling. At lunch Meenu told me: they're saying I copied my science project from the internet.

I did NOT. My Nani helped me cut the pictures, that's all, and I wrote everything myself. But I did look at one website for the volcano picture. So it's half true and half a lie and I don't even know how to explain it.

I felt hot and small. I wanted to hide under the bench, then to shout at all of them.

After school I told Omkar bhaiya, and he took me straight to Mummy. Mummy listened to everything and said, "You are not in trouble. We'll show Ma'am your notebook tomorrow, and I'm calling her tonight."

She did. I feel a tiny bit better.

— Ritu

qa.q: Who helped Ritu cut the pictures for the project?
qa.a: Her Nani.

qa.q: Why is Ritu so confused as well as upset?
qa.a: The rumour is half true, because Ritu did look at one website for a picture, so she feels ashamed and angry but doesn't know how to explain it.

qa.q: How did Omkar bhaiya and Mummy respond, and why did it help?
qa.a: Omkar took Ritu straight to Mummy, who listened, said Ritu was not in trouble, and called the teacher that night, so Ritu wasn't alone.

qa.q: How might Meenu have felt telling Ritu at lunch?
qa.a: She may have felt awkward but wanted to warn Ritu about what people were saying.

grounding: Ritu's diary shows her noticing giggles, learning a partly false rumour about her project and feeling shame and anger, then her family's same-day response.

passage:
On the bus home from school near Nashik, Reena saw two classmates look at her and giggle behind their hands. All day, whispering had stopped whenever she came near. Finally Indu said quietly, "They're saying your father went to jail, because of the police jeep at your house."
Reena's face burned. The jeep had come because someone stole their goat; her father had only given a statement. She wanted to jump off the bus and never go back. She also wanted to shove those girls off their seat. Her hands shook in her lap.
At home she would not eat. Aaji sat beside her on the charpai and asked gently, "Who hurt you today?" Reena told her everything. Aaji held her hand. "This is not your shame. Tomorrow I will come to school with you."

qa.q: Why had the police jeep come to Reena's house?
qa.a: It had come because someone stole their goat; her father had only given a statement.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when Indu told her what people were saying?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and angry, her face burning and hands shaking, wanting both to hide and to shove the girls.

qa.q: What helped Reena at this point, and what could come next?
qa.a: Aaji noticed, listened and told her it was not her shame; going to school together tomorrow can get the false story stopped by the teachers.

qa.q: What might Indu have been feeling when deciding to tell Reena?
qa.a: Indu may have felt uneasy and torn, wanting Reena to know what was being said even though it would hurt to hear.

grounding: Shows a girl noticing stares and giggles, learning a partly false story about her family, and feeling shame and anger.
